Fast and continuous growth in the market of energy storage systems has increased the demand for powerful cathode materials with excellent electrochemical characteristics. content: Emergence of the hazardous effects for the climate change forced the world governments to move quickly towards relying on different storage systems for the produced energy from renewable sources [1–3]. Therefore, the development of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have gained great attention because of their suitability for high energy and power density applications like electric vehicles and portable electronics [4,5]. Nowadays, the development of powerful cathode materials has become one of the main goals to improve the efficiency, cycle life and safety of commercial LIBs. One of these cathode materials that occupies the interest of research community; namely layered lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC) owing to its amazing capabilities for Li-ions storage, excellent chemical stability, extended life and affordable cost against lithium cobalt oxide (LCO) [6]. Although the ratio of Ni:Mn:Co in NMC cathode can be relatively changeable (e.g. NMC111, NMC532, NMC622 and NMC811), the NMC811 (LiNi0·8Mn0·1Co0·1O2) with the largest Ni content still exhibits the highest electrochemical storage capacity (∼200 mAhg−1) among the other chemical ratios of NMC cathode material [7,8]. However, capacity fading, low thermal stability and low capacity retention upon long-term cycling are being the most serious problems facing this kind of electrode materials [9,10]. There are several reasons responsible for happening this common degradation including (1) Li/Ni cation mixing [11], (2) reactivity of excess Li with H2O and CO2 forming undesirable Li2CO3 [12], (3) formation of insulating LiF layer due to side reactions with the electrolyte [13], (4) evolution of gases due to the electrolyte cracking [14], and (5) formation of thick layer of Li–O on the cathode surface upon electrolyte oxidation [15]. Two effective strategies (doping and coating) have been widely implemented to solve the aforementioned battery drawbacks. The chemical doping of (LiNi0·8Mn0·1Co0·1O2) with cations and anions of different elements (e.g. Mg, F, Cr, B, Na and Te) revealed a significant impact for improving the structural stability and electrochemical performance of NMC811-type batteries [16–20]. On the other hand, surface coating of NMC811 particles with various metal oxides such as WO3, TiO2, Li2MnO3, Li3PO4 and Li2SiO3 showed a considerable enhancement in the cyclic performance and thermal stability of NMC811 [21–25]. In addition, applying ultra thin films of Al2O3 or ZnO on the particles of NMC811 or NMC532 revealed a noticeable increase in the diffusion rate of Li + ions and decreased the polarization effect compared to pristine NMC samples [26,27]. On top of that, only three studies have been reported about the positive role of ZnAl2O4 coating film for enhancing the storage capabilities of spinel LiNi0·5Mn1·5O4, Mn-rich layered Li1·2Ni0·2Mn0·6O2, and olivine LiFePO4 cathode materials, respectively [28–30]. Interestingly, surface modification of Ni-rich NMC811 particles with ZnAl2O4 nanoparticles for Li-ion batteries has not been investigated so far. Compared with other related materials reported in previous literature, the ZnAl2O4 coating layer used for NMC811 particles is preferred due to its cheaper and easier fabrication at the nanoscale via an inexpensive and scalable strategy. Moreover, one might expect that implementing an outer shell of ZnAl2O4 on the top surface of NMC811 particles would achieve faster diffusion rates of Li + ions and a high degree of structural stability in addition to inhibiting electrolyte degradation in the cell. Thereby, in this paper a new surface-decorated layered cathode material (ZnAl2O4-coated LiNi0·8Mn0·1Co0·1O2) was designed via facile coprecipitation method. The induced changes in the crystallographic system and microstructure of coated NMC811 have been adequately explored. In addition, the surface analysis techniques EDS/mapping, HRTEM/SAED and XPS were performed to precisely characterize the coated material. The electrochemical performance of the promising coated- NMC811 cathode was studied using various electrochemical techniques including galvanostatic cycling (GC), cyclic voltammetry (CV) and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). 2

content: 2.1 Preparation of NMC811 and ZAO@NMC811 particles Facile solvothermal route was implemented to prepare pure LiNi0·8Mn0·1Co0·1O2 (NMC811) nanoparticles. The employed procedure includes dissolving certain amounts of the following salts: Ni(CH₃CO₂)₂·4H₂O (LOBA Chemie, 98.5%), Mn(CH₃CO₂)₂·4H₂O (LOBA Chemie, 99.5%) and Co(CH3CO2)2·4H2O (LOBA Chemie, 99%) in 60 ml ethyl alcohol/ethylene glycol solvents (1:1) according to Ni:Mn:Co molar ratio of 8:1:1. CH₃CO₂Li·2H₂O (Alfa Aeser, 98%) was added to this mixture with 10% excess larger than the stoichiometric amount of transition elements in order to compensate the loss of lithium at higher temperature. The solution was homogeneously mixed for 5 h and then transported to 100 ml stainless steel autoclave lined with Teflon and heated at 180 °C for 12 h. The obtained precursor was separated and dried using centrifuge and an electric oven, respectively. The obtained precursor was then subjected into two calcination stages; the first step at 450 °C/3 h and the second step at 800 °C/16 h under air atmospheric conditions to get the black powder of NMC811 using muffle furnace (Carbolite Gero Co. Ltd.). In order to prepare ZnAl2O4-coated NMC811 (ZAO@NMC811, 0.25 wt%), about 2.5 g of NMC811 particles was dispersed in 50 ml mixed solution of Zn(CH3CO2)2·2H2O (Sigma Aldrich, 99.5%) and Al(NO3)3·9H2O (Sigma Aldrich, 99%). Thereafter, the dissolved ions of zinc and aluminum were co-precipitated in the hydroxide form by adjusting the pH of this solution at 9 using few drops of NH4OH (33%). The Zn–Al hydroxide coated NMC811 particles were thoroughly filtered, washed and dried overnight at 120 °C to remove the residual moisture. Finally, ZnAl2O4-coated NMC811 particles were obtained after further calcination at 750 °C in air for 3 h. 2.2 Physicochemical characterization X-ray diffractometer (XRD) was used to analyze the crystal structures of the samples using Bruker AXS diffractometer (D8-ADVANCE) with Cu Ka radiation (λ = 1.54060 Å). The diffraction data were collected for 2θ values ranging from 10° to 80°, with a scanning rate of 0.4°min−1, step angle 0.02°. Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectrum (Model: AKX1200130) from Thermo Fisher Scientific Co Ltd., recorded between 4000 and 400 cm−1 in order to identify the characteristic functional groups of each sample. Raman spectroscopy was measured for ZAO@NMC811 using senterra dispersive Bruker micro-Raman (Germany) equipped with double frequency Nd:YAG laser at wavelength 532 nm to get more information about the chemical bonding and molecular interaction. High resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) Model: JEOL JEM2010 operating at 200 kV was conducted to discover the morphological and crystallographic features of the prepared electrode materials. Field emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM, QUANTA FEG-250) and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) were used to recognize the microstructure and chemical composition of the prepared particles. The attached elemental mapping unit was operated to show the distribution of each element. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) investigation was carried out via Thermo Scientific XPS (KALPHA surface analysis) instrument with an energy range of 0–1000 eV and an Al Kα source as an excitation source of 250 W power that was calibrated according to the C 1s line. 2.3 Electrochemical assessment of batteries The positive electrode slurry was made of 83 wt% active material, 10 wt% conductive additive super-P and 7 wt% polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF, Sigma Aldrich) binder completely dissolved in N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) solvent. The prepared conductive slurry was spread on Al sheet by the doctor blade technique and dried in a vacuum oven at 80 °C for 6 h. The net weight of active material on each electrode was about 4 mg cm−2. The electrodes were shaped into round discs using punching machine (16 mm diameter). 1 M LiPF6 in EC/DEC (1:1) solvents was employed as an electrolyte. Lithium chips (Sigma Aldrich, 99.9%) and micrporous polypropylene membranes were also utilized as negative electrodes and separators, respectively. The argon-filled MBRAUN glove box (humidity ≤1 ppm, Germany) was functionalized for assembling the two-electrode coin cells (CR 2032). The specific capacity of each cathode material was determined after galvanostatic cycling in the potential window (3.0–4.3 V) at 0.1 and 1 C rates. The cyclic voltammetric studies (CV) were swept at 0.05 mVs−1 between 2.8 and 4.3 V. The electrochemical impedance spectra (EIS) was measured in the frequency range 10 kHz–100 mHz at amplitude10 mV. 3

3.1 Physicochemical aspects Fig. 1 a shows the XRD patterns of the prepared NMC811 and ZAO@NMC811 cathode materials. Both samples indicates the formation of single phase of rhombohedral structure (R-3m space group) matching the diffraction peaks of layered hexagonal LiNiO2 structure (JCPDS 96–0063) [31,32]. The XRD pattern for spinel phase of pure ZnAl2O4 (JCPDS 05–0669) is shown in Fig. S1 in the supplementary data file. However, this phase cannot be identified in the ZAO@NMC811 sample because the existed amount (0.25 wt%) is still under the detection limit of XRD technique. The crystallite size L (nm) of the prepared powders can be calculated through Scherer equation as follow: (1) L = k λ β cos θ where (L) is the crystallite size, (λ) is the wave length of X-ray, ( β ) and ( θ ) are the full width at half-maximum (FWHM) of peak and the diffraction angle, (k) is the shape factor (k = 0.9). As a result, ZAO@NMC811 has larger crystallite size average ∼ 23 nm due to the coating of NMC811 particles (∼19.7 nm) with ZnAl2O4 nanoparticles (∼4.5 nm). In addition, the coating of NMC811 with ZnAl2O4 nanoparticles causes a slight shift in the diffraction peaks towards higher 2θ values, as shown in Fig. 1b. This peaks shift could be attributed to the shrinkage of lattice parameter and d-spacing which reduces the cell volume [24,30]. Table 1 reveals the changes in the crystallographic parameters before and after coating. It is also noticed that the ratio of I(003)/I(104) reflection intensity of ZAO@NMC811 is higher than pristine NMC811 suggesting higher cation distribution in the crystal lattice and lower degree of Li/Ni cation mixing [33,34]. The obtained crystallite size (L) and full width at half-maximum ( β ) can be used to calculate the dislocation density ( δ ) and the lattice micro-strain ( ε ) according to the following relations [35,36]: (2) T h e d i s l o c a t i o n d e n s i t y δ ( n m − 2 ) = 1 D 2 (3) T h e L a t t i c e m i c r o − s t r a i n ε = β 4 tan θ It can be inferred that the thin layer coating of NMC811 with Zn–Al oxide stabilizes the layered structure by reducing the lattice microstrain and dislocation density, as depicted in Table 1. The observed structure stabilization will minimize the phase transformation upon cycling leading to enhanced Li+ ions diffusion into the two-dimensional paths of the layered structure [37]. Fig. 2 a displays the FTIR absorption spectra of pristine NMC811 and ZAO@NMC811. It can be noticed that the absorption bands in the fingerprint region (<800 cm−1) of the bonds (Ni–O, Co–O and Mn–O) are very strong in the case of pristine NMC811, while the same bands of ZAO@NMC811 sample are much split and decreased in their intensity as well as significantly shifted towards lower frequencies [38,39]. The observed peaks at υ(866.8 cm−1) and υ(865.9 cm−1) for pure and coated NMC811 could be assigned to the presence of Li2CO3 impurities, which formed due to active surface reactions between Li + ions and atmospheric gases CO2/H2O [39,40]. The weak absorption bands at 674 and 1083.8 cm−1 are assigned to the stretching vibrations of Zn–O and Al–O bonds, respectively [41,42]. The presence of sharp peaks at 1430 and 1500 cm−1 might be attributed to the stretching vibrations of the C–O bond [43]. The weak bands at 1644 or 1630 cm−1 and the broad bands at 3412 or 3427 cm−1 are related to the bending modes of –OH groups found in the adsorbed water molecules [44]. A couple of weak bands at 2850 and 2920 cm−1 are existed in both samples due to the symmetric and asymmetric modes of aliphatic C–H bonds [45]. Fig. 2b shows a comparison between the Raman spectra of pristine NMC811 and the prepared ZAO@NMC811. The pure NMC811 reveals two principle strong bands in the regions 1000–1200 (related to C–H bonds) and 400-600 cm−1 (related to C–O bonds) which are characteristic of the layered structure of NMC811 indicating no phase transformation even after the coating process [46,47]. The noticeable red shift (i.e. longer wavelengths and lower wave numbers after surface modification of NMC811 with ZnAl2O4 coating layer could be attributed to the improved structural stability and lowering of the microstrain in the crystal lattice. Fig. 3 a and b show the difference in the morphologies of both prepared samples. The particles of pristine NMC811 (Fig. 3 a) have irregular polygonal shapes with sharp edges and the spaces are quietly separating these particles. Meanwhile, the ZnAl2O4-coated NMC811 particles (Fig. 3 b) have smoother and compact surface with regular rhombohedral shape. Additionally, SEM image of ZAO@NMC811 sample reveals larger particle size distribution range (0.7–1.23 μm) than that of pure NMC811 sample (0.67–1.2 μm). The EDS analysis for pristine NMC811 (Fig. S2a) indicates the approximate stoichiometric composition of its elements, while the corresponding elemental mapping (Fig. S2b) evinces the high homogenity between the atomic constituents. The EDS analysis of ZAO@NMC811 sample confirms the presence of all elements with closer ratio to the proposed chemical formula, as illustrated in Fig. 3c. The overall and selective elemental mapping for the coated NMC811 (Fig. 3d–j) indicate that all the constituting elements Zn, Al, Ni, Co, Mn, O are uniformly distributed in the layered structure. TEM micrographs for pure and coated NMC811 nanoparticles are compared in Fig. 4 a and d. It is observed that each particle of pure NMC811 (Fig. 4 a) reveals an irregular shape with different dimensions and an average particle size 70 nm, while the particle of ZAO@NMC811 is quite-spherical with an average particle size 110 nm (Fig. 4 b). In fact, the prepared coating film of ZnAl2O4 spinel nanomaterial is clearly adherent to the outer surface of pure NMC811 particles with an approximate thickness ∼ 9 nm. The uniformity, larger dimensions and higher homogenity of the coated NMC811 can be attributed to the existence of ZnAl2O4 film and the post-annealing of pure NMC811 at 750 °C/3 h during the in-situ formation of spinel phase coat. HRTEM images for pure NMC811 and coated NMC811 (Fig. 4 c and d) observe clear lattice fringes suggesting high crystallinity. Using the Fast Fourier Transformation (FFT) software for the magnified spot area of lattice fringes confirms the d-spacing value ∼ 0.46 nm of the plane (003) which belongs to the rhombohedral phase (R-3m space group), while the corresponding d-spacing of ZnAl2O4 spinel phase (Fd-3m space group) can be also detected by FTT software which equal 0.28 nm for the lattice plane (220). Similar HRTEM observations are reported for the surface modified NMC811 with FePO4 or Li3PO4 [24,48]. Fig. 4c depicts the exact selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern of the layered hexagonal structure of pure NMC811 [49]. In a comparative manner, the SAED pattern of ZAO@NMC811 (Fig. 4f) shows more numbers of shining rings and diffraction spots, indicating the existence of a secondary spinel crystal system (ZnAl2O4) associated with the primary layered phase of pure NMC811 lattice [50]. To confirm the presence of the ZnAl2O4 coating film and its influence on the electronic configuration of pristine NMC811 elements, the XPS technique was conducted on the prepared ZAO@NMC811 cathode material. Fig. S3, in the supplementary file, reveals the full XPS survey for pristine and ZnAl2O4-coated NMC811 cathode samples. In particular, the presence of Li+ cation is confirmed by the detection of Li 1s peak at 55.1 eV [51], as depicted in Fig. 5 a. The obtained Ni 2p spectra (Fig. 5b) consists of two main split peaks (Ni 2p3/2) at 855.7 eV and (Ni 2p1/2) at 873.2 eV. This peaks separation of 17.5 eV and the evolution of the shake-up satellite peak at 864.9 eV indicate the presence of trivalent Ni3+ cations [52]. The appearance of another spin-doublet around 855 and 873 eV also reveals the presence of Ni2+ cations. The broad XPS spectra of Mn 2p (Fig. 5c) with split signals around 637.5, 641.1 and 644.2 eV from the overall Mn 2p3/2 peak are related to the existence of Mn2+, Mn3+ and Mn4+ cations [53]. The satellite peak at binding energy 647.5 eV could be additional evidence for the formation of Mn4+ ions [53,54]. The XPS spectra of Co 2p (Fig. 5d) show the two main spin-doublets that are characteristic of Co 2p3/2 and Co 2p1/2, respectively. The first spin-doublet around 780.5 and 796 eV, and their associated shake-up satellite peaks at 790 and 803 eV unveil the existence of Co3+ cations [55,56]. The second spin-doublet appeared at 784.9 and 799 eV are relevant to the co-existence of Co4+ cations [57]. Fig. 5e comprises two main XPS spectra for Zn 2p around 1022.1 eV (Zn 2p1/2) and 1045.1 eV (Zn 2p3/2) with a separation distance of 23 eV, suggesting the existence of Zn2+ in the tetrahedral sites of the ZnAl2O4 film [58]. The evidence for the allocated Al3+ on the surface of NMC811 particles is recognized by the shallow XPS peak of Al 2p orbital between 71 and 77 eV [59], as exhibited in Fig. 5f. Fig. 5g represents O 1s XPS spectra that split into three signals to explain the way of bonding between the oxygen atom and lattice constituents. The first peak at 529.5 eV is assigned to the metal-oxygen bonding in the lattice of ZAO@NMC811 [60]. The second peak could be correlated to the Li–OH bonds, or the oxygen vacancies that existed in the crystal structure [61]. The third peak at 532.7 eV corresponds to the adsorbed H2O on the electrode material surface [62]. Fig. 5 (h) displays the XPS spectra of C 1s in ZAO@NMC811 consisting of three fitting peaks at binding energies of 284.7, 287.3 and 289.7 eV as a result of the existence of CO, C–O and C–C bonds, respectively [63]. 3.2 Electrochemical measurements Fig. 6 a depicts the first charge-discharge cycles of pristine NMC811 and ZAO@NMC811 upon cycling at 0.1C rate. It is obvious that the charge and discharge capacities of pristine NMC811 are about 209 and 173 mAhg−1, respectively. Meanwhile, the ZAO@NMC811 cell gained the highest charge and discharge capacities of about 221 and 188.5 mAhg−1, respectively. Moreover, the discharge curve of ZAO@NMC811 revealed a plateau shape at a higher voltage (3.7 V) than that (3.6 V) of pristine NMC811. Likely, the charge curve of ZAO@NMC811 exhibited a lower voltage (3.8 V) in the plateau region than that (3.9 V) of pristine NMC811. In more precise terms, the corresponding coulombic efficiency was increased from 82.7% to 84.5% by coating the NMC811 with a thin layer of ZnAl2O4. Such enhancement in the storage capacity could be related to the forbidden side interactions between the fluorinated electrolyte and the transition metal cations of the cathode [29]. Besides, the buffering effect of the nano-ZnAl2O4 ceramic shell on the cathode-electrolyte interphase (CEI) layer makes the pristine NMC811 more stable and capable for long-term cycling [30,64]. The charge and discharge processes that take place inside both cells can be interpreted by applying the CV test at 0.05 mV−1 between 2.8 and 4.3 V, as illustrated in Fig. 6b. The obtained CV plots disclose three couples of redox peaks for both cells which are characteristic for the layered NMC811 cathode materials. The detected primary oxidation/reduction couple of peaks in each cell are associated to three phase transitions (I/I’:hexagonal-1 to monoclinic phase, II/II’: monoclinic to hexagonal-2, and III/III’: hexagonal-2 to hexagonal-3) [65,66]. The potential difference between the first anodic and cathodic peaks (I/I’)is significantly reduced from 0.41 V for pure NMC811 to 0.16 V for ZAO@NMC811. This significant reduction in the separation potential means that the formed ZnAl2O4 outer-shell layer inhibits the phase transformation of hexagonal NMC811 into monoclinic phase, revealing better structure stability [67]. Moreover, the redox peaks of coated NMC811 demonstrate larger current density due to the polarization decrease between the NMC811 particles as well as the boosted hosting capability of NMC811 material for more Li+ ions intercalation on the active sites of the electrode surface [68]. The cyclability test was investigated for both cathode materials up to 100 cycles at 1 C within the potential range 3.0–4.3 V as plotted in Fig. 6c.
